title: Medical Interpreter Certification Standards & AI: July 2026
summary: Board certification for medical interpreters tests accuracy and terminology. See how AI interpretation holds up against the same quality bar. July 2026.
body_markdown:
###


The National Board of Certification for Medical Interpreters written exam covers 51 questions in English, with 61% of content weighted toward medical terminology and clinical specialties. The remaining 28% covers interpreter roles, ethics, and professional standards, so a candidate cannot pass on language skill alone.


###


Both the NBCMI Certified Medical Interpreter (CMI) and the CCHI Certified Healthcare Interpreter (CHI) signal the same baseline: 40 hours of formal training, verified bilingual proficiency, and a passed exam. The meaningful difference is the oral exam format, where CCHI adds simultaneous interpreting and NBCMI focuses on consecutive and sight translation; for most hospital procurement decisions, either credential meets the qualified interpreter standard under Section 1557.


###


CCHI offers the CoreCHI credential for language pairs that lack a full oral performance exam, which covers written knowledge but not live interpreting. Full oral exams through NBCMI exist only for Spanish, Mandarin, Cantonese, Russian, Korean, and Vietnamese, meaning patients who speak other languages have never had access to a fully board-certified interpreter, regardless of your staffing policies.


###


No. The 40-hour medical interpreter training requirement is a credentialing standard set by NBCMI and CCHI for professional certification, and no AI tool satisfies it. Opalite is a real-time AI medical interpretation tool designed to give healthcare organizations instant language access across more than 150 languages; it works alongside a certified interpreter program, covering volume, after-hours gaps, and languages where no certified interpreter pathway exists.


###


The per-minute billing model means your budget absorbs more than talk time: connection waits, physical exam silences, and documentation pauses all run on the meter. Carolinas Healthcare System spent $3.3 million on contract interpreter expenses in a single year, with interpretation representing more than half its total language services budget. Organizations that shift routine encounters to AI interpretation can reduce that spend by more than 50%, reserving certified human interpreters for high-complexity and high-risk encounters where their judgment is irreplaceable.
